first.rationale:
Two of the three current problems are activation (-6%) and onboarding completion (-4%), which point at the funnel rather than at price. memory_86 is the most directly load-bearing inherited claim for that diagnosis, so it is the one worth spending the single verification pull on: it is stated in terms of proxy outcomes (completion rate, time-to-value, 'early product adoption') rather than qualified revenue or retention, and I want the original record to see the horizon, the segment, and whether any revenue-quality metric was tracked at all. If the archive shows the lift was measured only at week one on self-serve accounts, the memory supports a funnel fix but does not by itself support the primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, and I would want the experiment instrumented for downstream conversion rather than completion.

I am deliberately not choosing promotional_pricing despite the competitor's entry pricing. memory_73 is real but it is the highest downstream-value-risk option here: discount-led acquisition into a price-sensitive SMB segment under competitive pressure tends to buy volume that anchors low, churns, and degrades the qualified-revenue number the objective actually targets. Matching a competitor's price move also concedes the pricing frame, and it is the hardest action to reverse. memory_31 and memory_91 point the same direction as memory_86 but at adjacent stages (signup fields, in-product nudges) and would be the fallbacks if verification undercuts memory_86; memory_57 and memory_44 address segments that are not where the current decline is showing.

Flagging downstream value risk even for the chosen action: removing onboarding steps can strip qualification and setup signal, producing more activated accounts that are worse-fit, so the guardrails should include fit/qualification and a retention read, not just completion. All the inherited memories are consolidated summaries with archived sources and none carry an effect size, sample, or duration; they are also 15-64 days stale and predate the current competitive environment, so I am treating them as directional priors rather than settled facts. Standard experiment scale with a holdout, because the action is low-blast-radius and reversible, but I will not scale it broadly on a single verified summary.

final.rationale:
Verification came back clean and strengthened the case: exp_86 recorded completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, and 30-day retention +3%. The retention figure matters most, because it is the one number that pushes this past a pure proxy result — shortening onboarding did not just move accounts through a funnel faster, it produced accounts that were still there a month later. That is the closest thing in the inherited record to evidence of durable rather than cosmetic gain, and it directly addresses my main worry that stripping onboarding steps would strip qualification signal and yield worse-fit activations.

The fit to the current situation is strong. Onboarding completion is down 4% and activation is down 6%; exp_86 is a verified intervention aimed squarely at both, with memory_31 (signup field reduction) and memory_91 (in-product activation nudges) pointing the same direction as corroborating but unverified priors. I am running onboarding rather than those two because it is the one I actually pulled the source record for.

I am still declining promotional_pricing even though the competitor's entry pricing is the loudest signal in the situation. memory_73 remains unverified, and discount-led acquisition into a price-sensitive SMB segment is the option most likely to buy churn-prone volume, anchor the segment low, and erode the qualified-revenue objective while being the hardest move to walk back. Losing price-shopping accounts to a competitor is a cheaper outcome than repricing the base. Fixing the funnel improves the value delivered per account, which is the more defensible answer to price pressure with one slot.

Remaining uncertainty, held explicitly: exp_86 still carries no qualified-revenue or expansion metric, and 30 days is not long-term. The record has no sample size or segment breakdown, and it is 24 days stale, predating the current competitive environment — a shortened flow may behave differently when incoming SMB traffic is more price-motivated and less committed. So: standard experiment with a holdout, not broad rollout. Guardrails instrumented on fit/qualification of activated accounts, downstream conversion to paid, and retention read at 30 and 60 days rather than completion rate alone. If activation rises while account quality or paid conversion falls, that is a stop signal, not a win, and I will not let a completion-rate lift alone justify scaling this.
